extracted.subtask_description: Exercises and explanatory guidelines for resolving curve and surface singularities via blow-ups, analyzing transforms/exceptions/divisors, and the foundations/construction of Tor and derived functors. Includes examples, classification remarks (ADE/Dynkin), and technical lemmas about blow-ups, line bundles, and cohomological tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper transform of cuspidal curve y^2 = x^3
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the proper transform of the cuspidal curve C given by y^2 = x^3 in the plane A^2. Show that it is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the proper transform of C meets the exceptional divisor E at one point, and is tangent to E there. (This is an explicit exercise — produce the transform under the blow-up at the origin and check regularity and tangency conditions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve y^2 = x^{n+1} by successive blow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the singularity y^2 = x^{n+1} in A^2 by first blowing up its singular point, then considering its proper transform and deciding what to do next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your solution should proceed by iteratively blowing up singular points of the proper transform until regular; the analysis depends only on the power-series expansion (not the exact equation). Compare with n=1 case for guidance; see later Definition 29.3.C for a precise notion of A_n curve singularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow up cone z^2 = x^2 + y^2 at origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Blow up the cone point z^2 = x^2 + y^2 at the origin. Show that the resulting surface is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the exceptional divisor is isomorphic to P^1. Remark: check the normal bundle to this P^1 (it is O(-2) here, unlike O(-1) in the case of blowing up a point on a smooth surface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve surface singularity z^2 = y^2 + x^{n+1}
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the singularity z^2 = y^2 + x^{n+1} in A^3 by first blowing up its singular point, then considering its proper transform and deciding subsequent blow-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the surface analogue of the curve exercise; performing sequential blow-ups of singular points will desingularize. The resulting singularities are called A_n surface singularities (make precise later). The exercise is time consuming but demonstrates explicit resolution by hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADE-surface singularity classification via exceptional divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: When you minimally desingularize ADE surface singularities by sequential blow-ups and inspect the arrangement of exceptional divisors and their intersections, you obtain the corresponding Dynkin diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the graph whose vertices correspond to exceptional divisors and join two vertices if the corresponding divisors meet; the underlying graph will match the Dynkin diagram (examples: D_n and E6,E7,E8 given by specified local equations). See Figure 22.2 and Remark 27.4.4 for further context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Hironaka's theorem for resolution in characteristic 0
rubrics_metrics.description: In characteristic 0, any variety X can be resolved by a sequence of blow-ups where each blow-up is along a regular subvariety lying in the singular locus of the previous stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Hironaka's theorem; for dimension 1 and 2, proofs are referenced later. In positive characteristic full resolution is not known in general; de Jong's Alteration Theorem gives an alternative producing a proper generically-finite separable map from a regular variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blowing up nonreduced subschemes can create singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that blowing up a nonreduced subscheme of a regular scheme can give a singular result (example: blow up V(y, x^2) in Spec k[x,y] = A^2 yields an A_1 surface singularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit counterexample — do the blow-up computation and check singularity of the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desingularize tacnode y^2 = x^4 by a single blow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Desingularize the tacnode y^2 = x^4, not in two steps, but in a single step by blowing up the ideal (y, x^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the non-obvious center (y, x^2) to blow up and verify the proper transform is regular; this demonstrates that suitable choice of blow-up center can shorten resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up of non-Cartier codimension-1 locus may still be isomorphism away from point
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is the cone x^2 + y^2 = z^2 and X is the line x=0, y=z on Y, then Bl_X Y is regular, and the blow-up morphism is an isomorphism away from the cone point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates blowing up a codimension-1 locus that is not an effective Cartier divisor globally but is Cartier away from a point; analyze local behavior to show isomorphism off the cone point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of a function at a regular point
rubrics_metrics.description: Define multiplicity of a function f at a regular point p of a locally Noetherian scheme X as the largest m such that f lies in the m-th power of the maximal ideal in O_{X,p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to detect singularities: V(f) is singular at p iff multiplicity m > 1. This notion is used to compute multiplicities appearing in transforms under blow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of exceptional divisor in total transform
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplicity of the exceptional divisor in the total transform of a subscheme Z of A^n when blowing up the origin equals the smallest multiplicity (at the origin) of a defining equation of Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for nodal and cuspidal curves, the exceptional divisor appears with multiplicity 2. Use local equations and their minimal vanishing order to compute the exceptional multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of birational map P^2 ↔ product via blow-ups (Exercise 22.4.K)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two distinct points p,q in P^2 and a third point r, describe the birational map related to blowing up points and interpreting points as pairs of lines through those points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider families of lines through p and q. Parametrizing choices of lines corresponds to P^1×P^1; analyze how points in P^2 correspond to such pairs, and study exceptional loci where correspondence fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-ups resolve base loci of rational maps to projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a scheme Y, an invertible sheaf L, and sections s0,...,sn of L, the rational map defined away from the base locus X = V(s0,...,sn) extends uniquely to a morphism Bl_X Y → P^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely the extension corresponds to the invertible sheaf (β^*L)(-E_XY) on Bl_X Y, where β is the blow-up morphism. Proof: work on affine opens where L is trivial; uniqueness may use Exercise 10.2.G. Blowing up the base scheme yields a base-point-free linear series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of pulled-back linear series and base locus removal
rubrics_metrics.description: The linear series on Y pulls back to one on Bl_X Y; the base locus pulls back to EXY, an effective Cartier divisor which can be divided out from β^*s_i to remove base points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows blowing up is the minimal modification removing base locus. If X is Cartier already, base locus removal can be done by dividing out X directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection P^n → P^{n-1} resolved by blowing up a point
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational projection P^n --> P^{n-1} given by forgetting a coordinate is resolved by blowing up the center point p; the invertible sheaf giving the map becomes β^*(O_{P^n}(1)) ⊗ O(-E_pY).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit example of Exercise 22.4.L and the Blow-up Closure Lemma 22.2.6; apply coordinate charts to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving pencils of cubics: blow up basepoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two general cubic equations C1 and C2 in three variables defining smooth plane cubics that meet in 9 points, the rational map [C1,C2] : P^2 → P^1 is resolved by blowing up those 9 basepoints, yielding (generically) an elliptic fibration Bl_{p1,...,p9} P^2 → P^1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Bertini to ensure smoothness and compute base locus as the 9 intersection points. This is an illustrative example rather than a complete argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow up six general points gives cubic surface embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing up six general points p1,...,p6 in P^2 (where cubics vanish at them) resolves a rational map P^2 → P^3, and the resulting morphism gives a closed embedding of Bl_{p1,...,p6} P^2 as a smooth cubic surface in P^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a classical fact; the argument in the text is only sketched — consult Section 27.4.2 for a complete discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph of a rational map equals blow-up of base locus
rubrics_metrics.description: If s0,...,sn are sections of an invertible sheaf L on an integral scheme X (not all zero), producing a rational map φ: X --> P^n, then the graph of φ is isomorphic to Bl_{V(s0,...,sn)} X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercise asks to give an isomorphism between the graph and the indicated blow-up; the statement holds in general without needing a base field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small resolution example for cone wz = xy
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the rational map from Spec k[w,x,y,z]/(wz-xy) (the cone over a quadric) to P^1 by blowing up the base locus w=x=0: the result X is isomorphic away from the cone point and the preimage of the cone point is P^1 of codimension 2 (a 'small' resolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: factor the map via the quadric Q in P^3 and project to one factor; compare alternatives to see non-uniqueness of small resolutions (Atiyah flop). Analyze how V(w,x) is not principal or even locally principal here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-isomorphic small resolutions and Atiyah flop
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be different small resolutions X and X' of the same singularity (both isomorphisms away from the origin with fiber P^1 over the origin) that are not isomorphic to each other; the birational map X ⇄ X' is called the Atiyah flop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show there is no morphism X → X' making the natural diagram commute; this illustrates subtleties of small resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak factorization theorem for birational maps (char 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two birational varieties X and Y in characteristic 0 may be related by a sequence of blow-ups and blow-downs along smooth centers (weak factorization theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precisely, exist intermediate varieties X0,...,Xn and morphisms between successive Xi that are blow-ups of smooth subvarieties. This is a structural result about birational geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard group change under blow-up of a point on a projective surface
rubrics_metrics.description: For X a regular projective surface and p a k-point, with β: Bl_p X → X and exceptional divisor E, there is an exact sequence 0 → Z [E] → Pic(Bl_p X) → Pic(Bl_p X  ackslash E) → 0, and Pic(Bl_p X) ≅ Pic X ⊕ Z, with E^2 = -1 (E is a (-1)-curve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use earlier results (14.2.8.1, 22.3.5) to show injection and splitting; describe how the intersection matrix on N1(Bl_p X) is obtained from that of Q(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform formula for Cartier divisors under blow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: If D is an effective Cartier divisor on X and mult_p D its multiplicity at p, and D' the proper transform, then π^*D = D' + (mult_p D) E as effective Cartier divisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More precisely, the product of the local equation for D' and the (mult_p D)-th power of the local equation for E equals the local equation for π^*D. Deduce π^* O_X(D) ≅ O_{Bl_p X}(D') ⊗ O_{Bl_p X}(E)^{⊗ mult_p D}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of canonical bundle under blow-up (surface case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = Bl(0,0) A^2 with π: X → A^2 and KY generated by dx ∧ dy, the pullback π^*(dx ∧ dy) vanishes to order 1 along the exceptional divisor E, giving K_X ≅ (π^* K_Y)(E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute in local chart U where line not vertical (y = m x), express dx ∧ dy = x (dx ∧ dm) and read off vanishing order along x=0 (E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional divisor multiplicity in general and blow-up along smooth center
rubrics_metrics.description: In dimension n, the exceptional divisor appears with multiplicity (n-1) in the pullback of a volume form; more generally, if Z is a smooth m-dimensional subvariety of a smooth n-dimensional Y and β : X = Bl_Z Y, then K_X ≅ (β^* K_Y)((n-m-1) E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: choose local generators of m/m^2 and lift them to compute dx_1∧...∧dx_n and count vanishing along E. Refer to Exercises 22.4.R and 22.4.S for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use blow-ups to cover quasiprojective varieties by affine opens
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a quasiprojective k-variety of dimension n, there is a construction using blowing up the complement in its projective closure to obtain a projective Y' = Bl_Z Y which can be covered by n+1 affine opens; thus X can be covered by n+1 affine opens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let Y be projective closure of X and put a subscheme structure on complement; blow it up to get Y' projective and affine cover of size n+1; restrict to X to get affine cover. Note: this fails for non-quasiprojective varieties (examples exist requiring arbitrarily many affines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensional vanishing for quasiprojective varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a quasiprojective k-scheme of dimension d and F any quasi-coherent sheaf on X, then H^i(X, F) = 0 for i > d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the affine cover by n+1 opens obtained via blow-ups and Theorem 18.2.6; this is Exercise 22.4.T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformation to the normal cone construction and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Given Y a k-variety and X ⊂ Y closed subscheme, the blow-up β: Bl_{X×{0}}(Y×P^1) → Y×P^1 composed with projection to P^1 gives the deformation to the normal cone: the exceptional divisor is the projective completion of the normal cone; the fiber over nonzero points is canonically isomorphic to Y, and the fiber over 0 is the normal cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish that π^*(0) is scheme-theoretic union of Bl_X Y and the projective completion of the normal cone, intersecting along EXY. This flat family degenerates Y to the normal cone and is useful in intersection-theoretic arguments (Fulton–MacPherson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and construction of Tor via free/projective resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: For A-modules M,N, take a (free/projective) resolution R of N and tensor it with M; Tor^A_i(M,N) is defined as the homology of M ⊗_A R at the ith stage. This construction is independent of the chosen resolution (up to canonical isomorphism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: build a free resolution, truncate, tensor with M (right-exactness issues), show independence via lifting maps between resolutions and homotopies (use axiom of choice). For N free, Tor_i = 0 for i>0. The connecting homomorphisms give long exact sequences for Tor induced by short exact sequences of modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long exact sequence for Tor functors
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a short exact sequence 0 → N' → N → N'' → 0 of A-modules, there is a long exact sequence ... → Tor^A_i(M,N') → Tor^A_i(M,N) → Tor^A_i(M,N'') → Tor^A_{i-1}(M,N') → ... → M⊗_A N' → M⊗_A N → M⊗_A N'' → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by taking projective resolutions of N' and N'' and using the horseshoe construction to build a resolution of N; then truncate, tensor with M and take homology. Verify naturality and independence of choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness characterized by vanishing Tor
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module M is flat iff Tor^A_i(M,N) = 0 for all i>0 and all A-modules N (equivalently Tor^A_1(M,N)=0 for all N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the definition of Tor via resolutions and the right-exactness of tensor to show equivalence. See Exercise 23.1.D for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on symmetry of Tor
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Tor^A_0(M,N) is symmetric (tensor product), for i>0 the symmetry Tor^A_i(M,N) ≅ Tor^A_i(N,M) is not automatic from the construction and will be established later (Exercise 23.3.A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume symmetry until proved; computations and exercises sometimes rely on later identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: General derived functors via projective/injective resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a right-exact covariant functor from an abelian category with enough projectives to another abelian category, define left derived functors L_i F by applying F to a projective resolution and taking homology; analogously define right derived functors using injective resolutions for left-exact functors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All arguments for Tor generalize: need enough projectives (or injectives) and that F respects products (additivity) so that applying F to the short exact 'horseshoe' resolution preserves exactness of columns. See Exercises 23.2.C–23.2.E for Ext and dual constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ext functors as right-derived Hom
rubrics_metrics.description: Ext^i_A(M,N) can be defined either as the ith right-derived functor of Hom(-, N) applied to M (using projective resolutions) or as the ith right-derived functor of Hom(M, -) applied to N (using injective resolutions); the two definitions agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and use the corresponding long exact sequences for Ext; finiteness properties follow in Noetherian settings (Exercise 23.2.F). Equivalence of definitions is proved later (Exercise 23.3.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective and injective objects and enough injectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Projective objects P are those lifting maps against surjections; equivalently every short exact sequence 0 → A → B → P → 0 splits. An abelian category has enough projectives/injectives if every object admits a surjection from a projective / an injection into an injective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For modules: projective modules are direct summands of free modules; projectives are flat. The category Mod_A has enough injectives (Exercises 23.2.G–23.2.K sketch construction via Hom_Z(A, Q) with Q divisible/injective over Z). Z-modules are injective iff divisible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal δ-functor axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: A (cohomological) δ-functor from an abelian category A to B is a collection of additive functors T^i : A → B with connecting morphisms δ^i : T^i(A'') → T^{i+1}(A') associated to every short exact sequence 0 → A' → A → A'' → 0, such that the long sequence formed is exact and T^0 is left-exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This abstracts key properties of derived functors and is useful when the category lacks enough injectives/projectives; it organizes long exact sequences and functoriality abstracts behind derived functors.
